702 
703 def encipher_hill(msg, key, symbols=None, pad="Q"):
704     r"""
705     Return the Hill cipher encryption of ``msg``.
706 
707     Notes
708     =====
709 
710     The Hill cipher [1]_, invented by Lester S. Hill in the 1920's [2]_,
711     was the first polygraphic cipher in which it was practical
712     (though barely) to operate on more than three symbols at once.
713     The following discussion assumes an elementary knowledge of
714     matrices.
715 
716     First, each letter is first encoded as a number starting with 0.
717     Suppose your message `msg` consists of `n` capital letters, with no
718     spaces. This may be regarded an `n`-tuple M of elements of
719     `Z_{26}` (if the letters are those of the English alphabet). A key
720     in the Hill cipher is a `k x k` matrix `K`, all of whose entries
721     are in `Z_{26}`, such that the matrix `K` is invertible (i.e., the
722     linear transformation `K: Z_{N}^k \rightarrow Z_{N}^k`
723     is one-to-one).
724 
725     ALGORITHM:
726 
727         INPUT:
728 
729             ``msg``: plaintext message of `n` upper-case letters
730 
731             ``key``: a `k x k` invertible matrix `K`, all of whose
732             entries are in `Z_{26}` (or whatever number of symbols
733             are being used).
734 
735             ``pad``: character (default "Q") to use to make length
736             of text be a multiple of ``k``
737 
738         OUTPUT:
739 
740             ``ct``: ciphertext of upper-case letters
741 
742         STEPS:
743             0. Number the letters of the alphabet from 0, ..., N
744             1. Compute from the string ``msg`` a list ``L`` of
745                corresponding integers. Let ``n = len(L)``.
746             2. Break the list ``L`` up into ``t = ceiling(n/k)``
747                sublists ``L_1``, ..., ``L_t`` of size ``k`` (with
748                the last list "padded" to ensure its size is
749                ``k``).
750             3. Compute new list ``C_1``, ..., ``C_t`` given by
751                ``C[i] = K*L_i`` (arithmetic is done mod N), for each
752                ``i``.
753             4. Concatenate these into a list ``C = C_1 + ... + C_t``.
754             5. Compute from ``C`` a string ``ct`` of corresponding
755                letters. This has length ``k*t``.
756 
757     References
758     ==========
759 
760     .. [1] en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hill_cipher
761     .. [2] Lester S. Hill, Cryptography in an Algebraic Alphabet,
762        The American Mathematical Monthly Vol.36, June-July 1929,
763        pp.306-312.
764 
765     See Also
766     ========
767     decipher_hill
768 
769     """
770     assert key.is_square
771     assert len(pad) == 1
772     msg, pad, A = _prep(msg, pad, symbols)
773     map = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(A)}
774     P = [map[c] for c in msg]
775     N = len(A)
776     k = key.cols
777     n = len(P)
778     m, r = divmod(n, k)
779     if r:
780         P = P + [map[pad]]*(k - r)
781         m += 1
782     rv = ''.join([A[c % N] for j in range(m) for c in
783         list(key*Matrix(k, 1, [P[i]
784         for i in range(k*j, k*(j + 1))]))])
785     return rv
786 
787 
788 def decipher_hill(msg, key, symbols=None):
789     """
790     Deciphering is the same as enciphering but using the inverse of the
791     key matrix.
792 
793     Examples
794     ========
795 
796     >>> from sympy.crypto.crypto import encipher_hill, decipher_hill
797     >>> from sympy import Matrix
798 
799     >>> key = Matrix([[1, 2], [3, 5]])
800     >>> encipher_hill("meet me on monday", key)
801     'UEQDUEODOCTCWQ'
802     >>> decipher_hill(_, key)
803     'MEETMEONMONDAY'
804 
805     When the length of the plaintext (stripped of invalid characters)
806     is not a multiple of the key dimension, extra characters will
807     appear at the end of the enciphered and deciphered text. In order to
808     decipher the text, those characters must be included in the text to
809     be deciphered. In the following, the key has a dimension of 4 but
810     the text is 2 short of being a multiple of 4 so two characters will
811     be added.
812 
813     >>> key = Matrix([[1, 1, 1, 2], [0, 1, 1, 0],
814     ...               [2, 2, 3, 4], [1, 1, 0, 1]])
815     >>> msg = "ST"
816     >>> encipher_hill(msg, key)
817     'HJEB'
818     >>> decipher_hill(_, key)
819     'STQQ'
820     >>> encipher_hill(msg, key, pad="Z")
821     'ISPK'
822     >>> decipher_hill(_, key)
823     'STZZ'
824 
825     If the last two characters of the ciphertext were ignored in
826     either case, the wrong plaintext would be recovered:
827 
828     >>> decipher_hill("HD", key)
829     'ORMV'
830     >>> decipher_hill("IS", key)
831     'UIKY'
832 
833     """
834     assert key.is_square
835     msg, _, A = _prep(msg, '', symbols)
836     map = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(A)}
837     C = [map[c] for c in msg]
838     N = len(A)
839     k = key.cols
840     n = len(C)
841     m, r = divmod(n, k)
842     if r:
843         C = C + [0]*(k - r)
844         m += 1
845     key_inv = key.inv_mod(N)
846     rv = ''.join([A[p % N] for j in range(m) for p in
847         list(key_inv*Matrix(
848         k, 1, [C[i] for i in range(k*j, k*(j + 1))]))])
849     return rv
850

855 def encipher_bifid(msg, key, symbols=None):
856     r"""
857     Performs the Bifid cipher encryption on plaintext ``msg``, and
858     returns the ciphertext.
859 
860     This is the version of the Bifid cipher that uses an `n \times n`
861     Polybius square.
862 
863         INPUT:
864 
865             ``msg``: plaintext string
866 
867             ``key``: short string for key; duplicate characters are
868             ignored and then it is padded with the characters in
869             ``symbols`` that were not in the short key
870 
871             ``symbols``: `n \times n` characters defining the alphabet
872             (default is string.printable)
873 
874         OUTPUT:
875 
876             ciphertext (using Bifid5 cipher without spaces)
877 
878     See Also
879     ========
880     decipher_bifid, encipher_bifid5, encipher_bifid6
881 
882     """
883     msg, key, A = _prep(msg, key, symbols, bifid10)
884     long_key = ''.join(uniq(key)) or A
885 
886     n = len(A)**.5
887     if n != int(n):
888         raise ValueError(
889             'Length of alphabet (%s) is not a square number.' % len(A))
890     N = int(n)
891     if len(long_key) < N**2:
892       long_key = list(long_key) + [x for x in A if x not in long_key]
893 
894     # the fractionalization
895     row_col = {ch: divmod(i, N) for i, ch in enumerate(long_key)}
896     r, c = zip(*[row_col[x] for x in msg])
897     rc = r + c
898     ch = {i: ch for ch, i in row_col.items()}
899     rv = ''.join((ch[i] for i in zip(rc[::2], rc[1::2])))
900     return rv
901 
902 
903 def decipher_bifid(msg, key, symbols=None):
904     r"""
905     Performs the Bifid cipher decryption on ciphertext ``msg``, and
906     returns the plaintext.
907 
908     This is the version of the Bifid cipher that uses the `n \times n`
909     Polybius square.
910 
911         INPUT:
912 
913             ``msg``: ciphertext string
914 
915             ``key``: short string for key; duplicate characters are
916             ignored and then it is padded with the characters in
917             ``symbols`` that were not in the short key
918 
919             ``symbols``: `n \times n` characters defining the alphabet
920             (default=string.printable, a `10 \times 10` matrix)
921 
922         OUTPUT:
923 
924             deciphered text
925 
926     Examples
927     ========
928 
929     >>> from sympy.crypto.crypto import (
930     ...     encipher_bifid, decipher_bifid, AZ)
931 
932     Do an encryption using the bifid5 alphabet:
933 
934     >>> alp = AZ().replace('J', '')
935     >>> ct = AZ("meet me on monday!")
936     >>> key = AZ("gold bug")
937     >>> encipher_bifid(ct, key, alp)
938     'IEILHHFSTSFQYE'
939 
940     When entering the text or ciphertext, spaces are ignored so it
941     can be formatted as desired. Re-entering the ciphertext from the
942     preceding, putting 4 characters per line and padding with an extra
943     J, does not cause problems for the deciphering:
944 
945     >>> decipher_bifid('''
946     ... IEILH
947     ... HFSTS
948     ... FQYEJ''', key, alp)
949     'MEETMEONMONDAY'
950 
951     When no alphabet is given, all 100 printable characters will be
952     used:
953 
954     >>> key = ''
955     >>> encipher_bifid('hello world!', key)
956     'bmtwmg-bIo*w'
957     >>> decipher_bifid(_, key)
958     'hello world!'
959 
960     If the key is changed, a different encryption is obtained:
961 
962     >>> key = 'gold bug'
963     >>> encipher_bifid('hello world!', 'gold_bug')
964     'hg2sfuei7t}w'
965 
966     And if the key used to decrypt the message is not exact, the
967     original text will not be perfectly obtained:
968 
969     >>> decipher_bifid(_, 'gold pug')
970     'heldo~wor6d!'
971 
972     """
973     msg, _, A = _prep(msg, '', symbols, bifid10)
974     long_key = ''.join(uniq(key)) or A
975 
976     n = len(A)**.5
977     if n != int(n):
978         raise ValueError(
979             'Length of alphabet (%s) is not a square number.' % len(A))
980     N = int(n)
981     if len(long_key) < N**2:
982         long_key = list(long_key) + [x for x in A if x not in long_key]
983 
984     # the reverse fractionalization
985     row_col = dict(
986         [(ch, divmod(i, N)) for i, ch in enumerate(long_key)])
987     rc = [i for c in msg for i in row_col[c]]
988     n = len(msg)
989     rc = zip(*(rc[:n], rc[n:]))
990     ch = {i: ch for ch, i in row_col.items()}
991     rv = ''.join((ch[i] for i in rc))
992     return rv
993

995 def bifid_square(key):
996     """Return characters of ``key`` arranged in a square.
997 
998     Examples
999     ========
1000 
1001     >>> from sympy.crypto.crypto import (
1002     ...    bifid_square, AZ, padded_key, bifid5)
1003     >>> bifid_square(AZ().replace('J', ''))
1004     Matrix([
1005     [A, B, C, D, E],
1006     [F, G, H, I, K],
1007     [L, M, N, O, P],
1008     [Q, R, S, T, U],
1009     [V, W, X, Y, Z]])
1010 
1011     >>> bifid_square(padded_key(AZ('gold bug!'), bifid5))
1012     Matrix([
1013     [G, O, L, D, B],
1014     [U, A, C, E, F],
1015     [H, I, K, M, N],
1016     [P, Q, R, S, T],
1017     [V, W, X, Y, Z]])
1018 
1019     See Also
1020     ========
1021     padded_key
1022     """
1023     A = ''.join(uniq(''.join(key)))
1024     n = len(A)**.5
1025     if n != int(n):
1026         raise ValueError(
1027             'Length of alphabet (%s) is not a square number.' % len(A))
1028     n = int(n)
1029     f = lambda i, j: Symbol(A[n*i + j])
1030     rv = Matrix(n, n, f)
1031     return rv
1032

1034 def encipher_bifid5(msg, key):
1035     r"""
1036     Performs the Bifid cipher encryption on plaintext ``msg``, and
1037     returns the ciphertext.
1038 
1039     This is the version of the Bifid cipher that uses the `5 \times 5`
1040     Polybius square. The letter "J" is ignored so it must be replaced
1041     with something else (traditionally an "I") before encryption.
1042 
1043     Notes
1044     =====
1045 
1046     The Bifid cipher was invented around 1901 by Felix Delastelle.
1047     It is a *fractional substitution* cipher, where letters are
1048     replaced by pairs of symbols from a smaller alphabet. The
1049     cipher uses a `5 \times 5` square filled with some ordering of the
1050     alphabet, except that "J" is replaced with "I" (this is a so-called
1051     Polybius square; there is a `6 \times 6` analog if you add back in
1052     "J" and also append onto the usual 26 letter alphabet, the digits
1053     0, 1, ..., 9).
1054     According to Helen Gaines' book *Cryptanalysis*, this type of cipher
1055     was used in the field by the German Army during World War I.
1056 
1057     ALGORITHM: (5x5 case)
1058 
1059         INPUT:
1060 
1061             ``msg``: plaintext string; converted to upper case and
1062             filtered of anything but all letters except J.
1063 
1064             ``key``: short string for key; non-alphabetic letters, J
1065             and duplicated characters are ignored and then, if the
1066             length is less than 25 characters, it is padded with other
1067             letters of the alphabet (in alphabetical order).
1068 
1069         OUTPUT:
1070 
1071             ciphertext (all caps, no spaces)
1072 
1073         STEPS:
1074             0. Create the `5 \times 5` Polybius square ``S`` associated
1075                to ``key`` as follows:
1076 
1077                 a) moving from left-to-right, top-to-bottom,
1078                    place the letters of the key into a `5 \times 5`
1079                    matrix,
1080                 b) if the key has less than 25 letters, add the
1081                    letters of the alphabet not in the key until the
1082                    `5 \times 5` square is filled.
1083 
1084             1. Create a list ``P`` of pairs of numbers which are the
1085                coordinates in the Polybius square of the letters in
1086                ``msg``.
1087             2. Let ``L1`` be the list of all first coordinates of ``P``
1088                (length of ``L1 = n``), let ``L2`` be the list of all
1089                second coordinates of ``P`` (so the length of ``L2``
1090                is also ``n``).
1091             3. Let ``L`` be the concatenation of ``L1`` and ``L2``
1092                (length ``L = 2*n``), except that consecutive numbers
1093                are paired ``(L[2*i], L[2*i + 1])``. You can regard
1094                ``L`` as a list of pairs of length ``n``.
1095             4. Let ``C`` be the list of all letters which are of the
1096                form ``S[i, j]``, for all ``(i, j)`` in ``L``. As a
1097                string, this is the ciphertext of ``msg``.
1098 
1099     Examples
1100     ========
1101 
1102     >>> from sympy.crypto.crypto import (
1103     ...     encipher_bifid5, decipher_bifid5)
1104 
1105     "J" will be omitted unless it is replaced with something else:
1106 
1107     >>> round_trip = lambda m, k: \
1108     ...     decipher_bifid5(encipher_bifid5(m, k), k)
1109     >>> key = 'a'
1110     >>> msg = "JOSIE"
1111     >>> round_trip(msg, key)
1112     'OSIE'
1113     >>> round_trip(msg.replace("J", "I"), key)
1114     'IOSIE'
1115     >>> j = "QIQ"
1116     >>> round_trip(msg.replace("J", j), key).replace(j, "J")
1117     'JOSIE'
1118 
1119     See Also
1120     ========
1121     decipher_bifid5, encipher_bifid
1122 
1123     """
1124     msg, key, _ = _prep(msg.upper(), key.upper(), None, bifid5)
1125     key = padded_key(key, bifid5)
1126     return encipher_bifid(msg, '', key)
1127 
1128 
1129 def decipher_bifid5(msg, key):
1130     r"""
1131     Return the Bifid cipher decryption of ``msg``.
1132 
1133     This is the version of the Bifid cipher that uses the `5 \times 5`
1134     Polybius square; the letter "J" is ignored unless a ``key`` of
1135     length 25 is used.
1136 
1137     INPUT:
1138 
1139         ``msg``: ciphertext string
1140 
1141         ``key``: short string for key; duplicated characters are
1142         ignored and if the length is less then 25 characters, it
1143         will be padded with other letters from the alphabet omitting
1144         "J". Non-alphabetic characters are ignored.

1146     OUTPUT:
1147 
1148         plaintext from Bifid5 cipher (all caps, no spaces)
1149 
1150     Examples
1151     ========
1152 
1153     >>> from sympy.crypto.crypto import encipher_bifid5, decipher_bifid5
1154     >>> key = "gold bug"
1155     >>> encipher_bifid5('meet me on friday', key)

1160     'MEETMEONMONDAY'
1161 
1162     """
1163     msg, key, _ = _prep(msg.upper(), key.upper(), None, bifid5)
1164     key = padded_key(key, bifid5)
1165     return decipher_bifid(msg, '', key)

1168 def bifid5_square(key=None):
1169     r"""
1170     5x5 Polybius square.
1171 
1172     Produce the Polybius square for the `5 \times 5` Bifid cipher.
1173 
1174     Examples
1175     ========
1176 
1177     >>> from sympy.crypto.crypto import bifid5_square
1178     >>> bifid5_square("gold bug")

1180     [G, O, L, D, B],

1182     [H, I, K, M, N],

1186     """

1188         key = bifid5
1189     else:
1190         _, key, _ = _prep('', key.upper(), None, bifid5)
1191         key = padded_key(key, bifid5)
1192     return bifid_square(key)

1294 def rsa_public_key(p, q, e):
1295     r"""
1296     Return the RSA *public key* pair, `(n, e)`, where `n`
1297     is a product of two primes and `e` is relatively
1298     prime (coprime) to the Euler totient `\phi(n)`. False
1299     is returned if any assumption is violated.
1300 
1301     Examples
1302     ========
1303 
1304     >>> from sympy.crypto.crypto import rsa_public_key
1305     >>> p, q, e = 3, 5, 7
1306     >>> rsa_public_key(p, q, e)
1307     (15, 7)
1308     >>> rsa_public_key(p, q, 30)
1309     False
1310 
1311     """
1312     n = p*q
1313     if isprime(p) and isprime(q):
1314         if p == q:
1315             SymPyDeprecationWarning(
1316                 feature="Using non-distinct primes for rsa_public_key",
1317                 useinstead="distinct primes",
1318                 issue=16162,
1319                 deprecated_since_version="1.4").warn()
1320             phi = p * (p - 1)
1321         else:
1322             phi = (p - 1) * (q - 1)
1323         if gcd(e, phi) == 1:
1324             return n, e
1325     return False
1326

1328 def rsa_private_key(p, q, e):
1329     r"""
1330     Return the RSA *private key*, `(n,d)`, where `n`
1331     is a product of two primes and `d` is the inverse of
1332     `e` (mod `\phi(n)`). False is returned if any assumption
1333     is violated.
1334 
1335     Examples
1336     ========
1337 
1338     >>> from sympy.crypto.crypto import rsa_private_key
1339     >>> p, q, e = 3, 5, 7
1340     >>> rsa_private_key(p, q, e)
1341     (15, 7)
1342     >>> rsa_private_key(p, q, 30)
1343     False
1344     """
1345     n = p*q
1346     if isprime(p) and isprime(q):
1347         if p == q:
1348             SymPyDeprecationWarning(
1349                 feature="Using non-distinct primes for rsa_public_key",
1350                 useinstead="distinct primes",
1351                 issue=16162,
1352                 deprecated_since_version="1.4").warn()
1353             phi = p * (p - 1)
1354         else:
1355             phi = (p - 1) * (q - 1)
1356         if gcd(e, phi) == 1:
1357             d = mod_inverse(e, phi)
1358             return n, d
1359     return False

1405 def kid_rsa_public_key(a, b, A, B):
1406     r"""
1407     Kid RSA is a version of RSA useful to teach grade school children
1408     since it does not involve exponentiation.
1409 
1410     Alice wants to talk to Bob. Bob generates keys as follows.
1411     Key generation:
1412 
1413     * Select positive integers `a, b, A, B` at random.
1414     * Compute `M = a b - 1`, `e = A M + a`, `d = B M + b`,
1415       `n = (e d - 1)//M`.
1416     * The *public key* is `(n, e)`. Bob sends these to Alice.
1417     * The *private key* is `(n, d)`, which Bob keeps secret.
1418 
1419     Encryption: If `p` is the plaintext message then the
1420     ciphertext is `c = p e \pmod n`.
1421 
1422     Decryption: If `c` is the ciphertext message then the
1423     plaintext is `p = c d \pmod n`.
1424 
1425     Examples
1426     ========
1427 
1428     >>> from sympy.crypto.crypto import kid_rsa_public_key
1429     >>> a, b, A, B = 3, 4, 5, 6
1430     >>> kid_rsa_public_key(a, b, A, B)
1431     (369, 58)
1432 
1433     """
1434     M = a*b - 1
1435     e = A*M + a
1436     d = B*M + b
1437     n = (e*d - 1)//M
1438     return n, e
1439 
1440 
1441 def kid_rsa_private_key(a, b, A, B):
1442     """
1443     Compute `M = a b - 1`, `e = A M + a`, `d = B M + b`,
1444     `n = (e d - 1) / M`. The *private key* is `d`, which Bob
1445     keeps secret.
1446 
1447     Examples
1448     ========
1449 
1450     >>> from sympy.crypto.crypto import kid_rsa_private_key
1451     >>> a, b, A, B = 3, 4, 5, 6
1452     >>> kid_rsa_private_key(a, b, A, B)
1453     (369, 70)
1454 
1455     """
1456     M = a*b - 1
1457     e = A*M + a
1458     d = B*M + b
1459     n = (e*d - 1)//M
1460     return n, d
1461

1463 def encipher_kid_rsa(msg, key):

1539 def encode_morse(msg, sep='|', mapping=None):
1540     """
1541     Encodes a plaintext into popular Morse Code with letters
1542     separated by `sep` and words by a double `sep`.
1543 
1544     References
1545     ==========
1546 
1547     .. [1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morse_code
1548 
1549     Examples
1550     ========
1551 
1552     >>> from sympy.crypto.crypto import encode_morse
1553     >>> msg = 'ATTACK RIGHT FLANK'
1554     >>> encode_morse(msg)
1555     '.-|-|-|.-|-.-.|-.-||.-.|..|--.|....|-||..-.|.-..|.-|-.|-.-'
1556 
1557     """
1558 
1559     mapping = mapping or char_morse
1560     assert sep not in mapping
1561     word_sep = 2*sep
1562     mapping[" "] = word_sep
1563     suffix = msg and msg[-1] in whitespace
1564 
1565     # normalize whitespace
1566     msg = (' ' if word_sep else '').join(msg.split())
1567     # omit unmapped chars
1568     chars = set(''.join(msg.split()))
1569     ok = set(mapping.keys())
1570     msg = translate(msg, None, ''.join(chars - ok))
1571 
1572     morsestring = []
1573     words = msg.split()
1574     for word in words:
1575         morseword = []
1576         for letter in word:
1577             morseletter = mapping[letter]
1578             morseword.append(morseletter)
1579 
1580         word = sep.join(morseword)
1581         morsestring.append(word)
1582 
1583     return word_sep.join(morsestring) + (word_sep if suffix else '')
1584

1586 def decode_morse(msg, sep='|', mapping=None):
1587     """
1588     Decodes a Morse Code with letters separated by `sep`
1589     (default is '|') and words by `word_sep` (default is '||)
1590     into plaintext.
1591 
1592     References
1593     ==========
1594 
1595     .. [1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morse_code
1596 
1597     Examples
1598     ========
1599 
1600     >>> from sympy.crypto.crypto import decode_morse
1601     >>> mc = '--|---|...-|.||.|.-|...|-'
1602     >>> decode_morse(mc)
1603     'MOVE EAST'
1604 
1605     """
1606 
1607     mapping = mapping or morse_char
1608     word_sep = 2*sep
1609     characterstring = []
1610     words = msg.strip(word_sep).split(word_sep)
1611     for word in words:
1612         letters = word.split(sep)
1613         chars = [mapping[c] for c in letters]
1614         word = ''.join(chars)
1615         characterstring.append(word)
1616     rv = " ".join(characterstring)
1617     return rv

1623 def lfsr_sequence(key, fill, n):
1624     r"""
1625     This function creates an lfsr sequence.
1626 
1627     INPUT:
1628 
1629         ``key``: a list of finite field elements,
1630             `[c_0, c_1, \ldots, c_k].`
1631 
1632         ``fill``: the list of the initial terms of the lfsr
1633             sequence, `[x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_k].`
1634 
1635         ``n``: number of terms of the sequence that the
1636             function returns.
1637 
1638     OUTPUT:
1639 
1640         The lfsr sequence defined by
1641         `x_{n+1} = c_k x_n + \ldots + c_0 x_{n-k}`, for
1642         `n \leq k`.
1643 
1644     Notes
1645     =====
1646 
1647     S. Golomb [G]_ gives a list of three statistical properties a
1648     sequence of numbers `a = \{a_n\}_{n=1}^\infty`,
1649     `a_n \in \{0,1\}`, should display to be considered
1650     "random". Define the autocorrelation of `a` to be
1651 
1652     .. math::
1653 
1654         C(k) = C(k,a) = \lim_{N\rightarrow \infty} {1\over N}\sum_{n=1}^N (-1)^{a_n + a_{n+k}}.
1655 
1656     In the case where `a` is periodic with period
1657     `P` then this reduces to
1658 
1659     .. math::
1660 
1661         C(k) = {1\over P}\sum_{n=1}^P (-1)^{a_n + a_{n+k}}.
1662 
1663     Assume `a` is periodic with period `P`.
1664 
1665     - balance:
1666 
1667       .. math::
1668 
1669         \left|\sum_{n=1}^P(-1)^{a_n}\right| \leq 1.
1670 
1671     - low autocorrelation:
1672 
1673        .. math::
1674 
1675          C(k) = \left\{ \begin{array}{cc} 1,& k = 0,\\ \epsilon, & k \ne 0. \end{array} \right.
1676 
1677       (For sequences satisfying these first two properties, it is known
1678       that `\epsilon = -1/P` must hold.)
1679 
1680     - proportional runs property: In each period, half the runs have
1681       length `1`, one-fourth have length `2`, etc.
1682       Moreover, there are as many runs of `1`'s as there are of
1683       `0`'s.
1684 
1685     References
1686     ==========
1687 
1688     .. [G] Solomon Golomb, Shift register sequences, Aegean Park Press,
1689        Laguna Hills, Ca, 1967
1690 
1691     Examples
1692     ========
1693 
1694     >>> from sympy.crypto.crypto import lfsr_sequence
1695     >>> from sympy.polys.domains import FF
1696     >>> F = FF(2)
1697     >>> fill = [F(1), F(1), F(0), F(1)]
1698     >>> key = [F(1), F(0), F(0), F(1)]
1699     >>> lfsr_sequence(key, fill, 10)
1700     [1 mod 2, 1 mod 2, 0 mod 2, 1 mod 2, 0 mod 2,
1701     1 mod 2, 1 mod 2, 0 mod 2, 0 mod 2, 1 mod 2]
1702 
1703     """
1704     if not isinstance(key, list):
1705         raise TypeError("key must be a list")
1706     if not isinstance(fill, list):
1707         raise TypeError("fill must be a list")
1708     p = key[0].mod
1709     F = FF(p)
1710     s = fill
1711     k = len(fill)
1712     L = []
1713     for i in range(n):
1714         s0 = s[:]
1715         L.append(s[0])
1716         s = s[1:k]
1717         x = sum([int(key[i]*s0[i]) for i in range(k)])
1718         s.append(F(x))
1719     return L       # use [x.to_int() for x in L] for int version
1720 
1721 
1722 def lfsr_autocorrelation(L, P, k):
1723     """
1724     This function computes the LFSR autocorrelation function.
1725 
1726     INPUT:
1727 
1728         ``L``: is a periodic sequence of elements of `GF(2)`.
1729         ``L`` must have length larger than ``P``.
1730 
1731         ``P``: the period of ``L``
1732 
1733         ``k``: an integer (`0 < k < p`)
1734 
1735     OUTPUT:
1736 
1737         the ``k``-th value of the autocorrelation of the LFSR ``L``
1738 
1739     Examples
1740     ========
1741 
1742     >>> from sympy.crypto.crypto import (
1743     ...     lfsr_sequence, lfsr_autocorrelation)
1744     >>> from sympy.polys.domains import FF
1745     >>> F = FF(2)
1746     >>> fill = [F(1), F(1), F(0), F(1)]
1747     >>> key = [F(1), F(0), F(0), F(1)]
1748     >>> s = lfsr_sequence(key, fill, 20)
1749     >>> lfsr_autocorrelation(s, 15, 7)
1750     -1/15
1751     >>> lfsr_autocorrelation(s, 15, 0)
1752     1
1753 
1754     """
1755     if not isinstance(L, list):
1756         raise TypeError("L (=%s) must be a list" % L)
1757     P = int(P)
1758     k = int(k)
1759     L0 = L[:P]     # slices makes a copy
1760     L1 = L0 + L0[:k]
1761     L2 = [(-1)**(L1[i].to_int() + L1[i + k].to_int()) for i in range(P)]
1762     tot = sum(L2)
1763     return Rational(tot, P)

1766 def lfsr_connection_polynomial(s):
1767     """
1768     This function computes the LFSR connection polynomial.
1769 
1770     INPUT:
1771 
1772         ``s``: a sequence of elements of even length, with entries in
1773         a finite field
1774 
1775     OUTPUT:
1776 
1777         ``C(x)``: the connection polynomial of a minimal LFSR yielding
1778         ``s``.
1779 
1780     This implements the algorithm in section 3 of J. L. Massey's
1781     article [M]_.
1782 
1783     References
1784     ==========
1785 
1786     .. [M] James L. Massey, "Shift-Register Synthesis and BCH Decoding."
1787         IEEE Trans. on Information Theory, vol. 15(1), pp. 122-127,
1788         Jan 1969.
1789 
1790     Examples
1791     ========
1792 
1793     >>> from sympy.crypto.crypto import (
1794     ...     lfsr_sequence, lfsr_connection_polynomial)
1795     >>> from sympy.polys.domains import FF
1796     >>> F = FF(2)
1797     >>> fill = [F(1), F(1), F(0), F(1)]
1798     >>> key = [F(1), F(0), F(0), F(1)]
1799     >>> s = lfsr_sequence(key, fill, 20)
1800     >>> lfsr_connection_polynomial(s)
1801     x**4 + x + 1
1802     >>> fill = [F(1), F(0), F(0), F(1)]
1803     >>> key = [F(1), F(1), F(0), F(1)]
1804     >>> s = lfsr_sequence(key, fill, 20)
1805     >>> lfsr_connection_polynomial(s)
1806     x**3 + 1
1807     >>> fill = [F(1), F(0), F(1)]
1808     >>> key = [F(1), F(1), F(0)]
1809     >>> s = lfsr_sequence(key, fill, 20)
1810     >>> lfsr_connection_polynomial(s)
1811     x**3 + x**2 + 1
1812     >>> fill = [F(1), F(0), F(1)]
1813     >>> key = [F(1), F(0), F(1)]
1814     >>> s = lfsr_sequence(key, fill, 20)
1815     >>> lfsr_connection_polynomial(s)
1816     x**3 + x + 1
1817 
1818     """
1819     # Initialization:
1820     p = s[0].mod
1821     x = Symbol("x")
1822     C = 1*x**0
1823     B = 1*x**0
1824     m = 1
1825     b = 1*x**0
1826     L = 0
1827     N = 0
1828     while N < len(s):
1829         if L > 0:
1830             dC = Poly(C).degree()
1831             r = min(L + 1, dC + 1)
1832             coeffsC = [C.subs(x, 0)] + [C.coeff(x**i)
1833                 for i in range(1, dC + 1)]
1834             d = (s[N].to_int() + sum([coeffsC[i]*s[N - i].to_int()
1835                 for i in range(1, r)])) % p
1836         if L == 0:
1837             d = s[N].to_int()*x**0
1838         if d == 0:
1839             m += 1
1840             N += 1
1841         if d > 0:
1842             if 2*L > N:
1843                 C = (C - d*((b**(p - 2)) % p)*x**m*B).expand()
1844                 m += 1
1845                 N += 1
1846             else:
1847                 T = C
1848                 C = (C - d*((b**(p - 2)) % p)*x**m*B).expand()
1849                 L = N + 1 - L

2231     without knowing its factorization.

1 """
2 Implementation of the trigsimp algorithm by Fu et al.
3 
4 The idea behind the ``fu`` algorithm is to use a sequence of rules, applied
5 in what is heuristically known to be a smart order, to select a simpler
6 expression that is equivalent to the input.
7 
8 There are transform rules in which a single rule is applied to the
9 expression tree. The following are just mnemonic in nature; see the
10 docstrings for examples.
11 
12     TR0 - simplify expression
13     TR1 - sec-csc to cos-sin
14     TR2 - tan-cot to sin-cos ratio
15     TR2i - sin-cos ratio to tan
16     TR3 - angle canonicalization
17     TR4 - functions at special angles
18     TR5 - powers of sin to powers of cos
19     TR6 - powers of cos to powers of sin
20     TR7 - reduce cos power (increase angle)
21     TR8 - expand products of sin-cos to sums
22     TR9 - contract sums of sin-cos to products
23     TR10 - separate sin-cos arguments
24     TR10i - collect sin-cos arguments
25     TR11 - reduce double angles
26     TR12 - separate tan arguments
27     TR12i - collect tan arguments
28     TR13 - expand product of tan-cot
29     TRmorrie - prod(cos(x*2**i), (i, 0, k - 1)) -> sin(2**k*x)/(2**k*sin(x))
30     TR14 - factored powers of sin or cos to cos or sin power
31     TR15 - negative powers of sin to cot power
32     TR16 - negative powers of cos to tan power
33     TR22 - tan-cot powers to negative powers of sec-csc functions
34     TR111 - negative sin-cos-tan powers to csc-sec-cot
35 
36 There are 4 combination transforms (CTR1 - CTR4) in which a sequence of
37 transformations are applied and the simplest expression is selected from
38 a few options.
39 
40 Finally, there are the 2 rule lists (RL1 and RL2), which apply a
41 sequence of transformations and combined transformations, and the ``fu``
42 algorithm itself, which applies rules and rule lists and selects the
43 best expressions. There is also a function ``L`` which counts the number
44 of trigonometric functions that appear in the expression.
45 
46 Other than TR0, re-writing of expressions is not done by the transformations.
47 e.g. TR10i finds pairs of terms in a sum that are in the form like
48 ``cos(x)*cos(y) + sin(x)*sin(y)``. Such expression are targeted in a bottom-up
49 traversal of the expression, but no manipulation to make them appear is
50 attempted. For example,
51 
52     Set-up for examples below:
53 
54     >>> from sympy.simplify.fu import fu, L, TR9, TR10i, TR11
55     >>> from sympy import factor, sin, cos, powsimp
56     >>> from sympy.abc import x, y, z, a
57     >>> from time import time
58 
59 >>> eq = cos(x + y)/cos(x)
60 >>> TR10i(eq.expand(trig=True))
61 -sin(x)*sin(y)/cos(x) + cos(y)
62 
63 If the expression is put in "normal" form (with a common denominator) then
64 the transformation is successful:
65 
66 >>> TR10i(_.normal())
67 cos(x + y)/cos(x)
68 
69 TR11's behavior is similar. It rewrites double angles as smaller angles but
70 doesn't do any simplification of the result.
71 
72 >>> TR11(sin(2)**a*cos(1)**(-a), 1)
73 (2*sin(1)*cos(1))**a*cos(1)**(-a)
74 >>> powsimp(_)
75 (2*sin(1))**a
76 
77 The temptation is to try make these TR rules "smarter" but that should really
78 be done at a higher level; the TR rules should try maintain the "do one thing
79 well" principle.  There is one exception, however. In TR10i and TR9 terms are
80 recognized even when they are each multiplied by a common factor:
81 
82 >>> fu(a*cos(x)*cos(y) + a*sin(x)*sin(y))
83 a*cos(x - y)
84 
85 Factoring with ``factor_terms`` is used but it it "JIT"-like, being delayed
86 until it is deemed necessary. Furthermore, if the factoring does not
87 help with the simplification, it is not retained, so
88 ``a*cos(x)*cos(y) + a*sin(x)*sin(z)`` does not become the factored
89 (but unsimplified in the trigonometric sense) expression:
90 
91 >>> fu(a*cos(x)*cos(y) + a*sin(x)*sin(z))
92 a*sin(x)*sin(z) + a*cos(x)*cos(y)
93 
94 In some cases factoring might be a good idea, but the user is left
95 to make that decision. For example:
96 
97 >>> expr=((15*sin(2*x) + 19*sin(x + y) + 17*sin(x + z) + 19*cos(x - z) +
98 ... 25)*(20*sin(2*x) + 15*sin(x + y) + sin(y + z) + 14*cos(x - z) +
99 ... 14*cos(y - z))*(9*sin(2*y) + 12*sin(y + z) + 10*cos(x - y) + 2*cos(y -
100 ... z) + 18)).expand(trig=True).expand()
101 
102 In the expanded state, there are nearly 1000 trig functions:
103 
104 >>> L(expr)
105 932
106 
107 If the expression where factored first, this would take time but the
108 resulting expression would be transformed very quickly:
109 
110 >>> def clock(f, n=2):
111 ...    t=time(); f(); return round(time()-t, n)
112 ...
113 >>> clock(lambda: factor(expr))  # doctest: +SKIP
114 0.86
115 >>> clock(lambda: TR10i(expr), 3)  # doctest: +SKIP
116 0.016
117 
118 If the unexpanded expression is used, the transformation takes longer but
119 not as long as it took to factor it and then transform it:
120 
121 >>> clock(lambda: TR10i(expr), 2)  # doctest: +SKIP
122 0.28
123 
124 So neither expansion nor factoring is used in ``TR10i``: if the
125 expression is already factored (or partially factored) then expansion
126 with ``trig=True`` would destroy what is already known and take
127 longer; if the expression is expanded, factoring may take longer than
128 simply applying the transformation itself.
129 
130 Although the algorithms should be canonical, always giving the same
131 result, they may not yield the best result. This, in general, is
132 the nature of simplification where searching all possible transformation
133 paths is very expensive. Here is a simple example. There are 6 terms
134 in the following sum:
135 
136 >>> expr = (sin(x)**2*cos(y)*cos(z) + sin(x)*sin(y)*cos(x)*cos(z) +
137 ... sin(x)*sin(z)*cos(x)*cos(y) + sin(y)*sin(z)*cos(x)**2 + sin(y)*sin(z) +
138 ... cos(y)*cos(z))
139 >>> args = expr.args
140 
141 Serendipitously, fu gives the best result:
142 
143 >>> fu(expr)
144 3*cos(y - z)/2 - cos(2*x + y + z)/2
145 
146 But if different terms were combined, a less-optimal result might be
147 obtained, requiring some additional work to get better simplification,
148 but still less than optimal. The following shows an alternative form
149 of ``expr`` that resists optimal simplification once a given step
150 is taken since it leads to a dead end:
151 
152 >>> TR9(-cos(x)**2*cos(y + z) + 3*cos(y - z)/2 +
153 ...     cos(y + z)/2 + cos(-2*x + y + z)/4 - cos(2*x + y + z)/4)
154 sin(2*x)*sin(y + z)/2 - cos(x)**2*cos(y + z) + 3*cos(y - z)/2 + cos(y + z)/2
155 
156 Here is a smaller expression that exhibits the same behavior:
157 
158 >>> a = sin(x)*sin(z)*cos(x)*cos(y) + sin(x)*sin(y)*cos(x)*cos(z)
159 >>> TR10i(a)
160 sin(x)*sin(y + z)*cos(x)
161 >>> newa = _
162 >>> TR10i(expr - a)  # this combines two more of the remaining terms
163 sin(x)**2*cos(y)*cos(z) + sin(y)*sin(z)*cos(x)**2 + cos(y - z)
164 >>> TR10i(_ + newa) == _ + newa  # but now there is no more simplification
165 True
166 
167 Without getting lucky or trying all possible pairings of arguments, the
168 final result may be less than optimal and impossible to find without
169 better heuristics or brute force trial of all possibilities.

246         elif isinstance(rv, csc):

293     >>> from sympy.abc import x, a
294     >>> from sympy import sin, cos
295     >>> TR2i(sin(x)/cos(x))
296     tan(x)
297 
298     Powers of the numerator and denominator are also recognized
299 
300     >>> TR2i(sin(x)**2/(cos(x) + 1)**2, half=True)
301     tan(x/2)**2
302 
303     The transformation does not take place unless assumptions allow
304     (i.e. the base must be positive or the exponent must be an integer
305     for both numerator and denominator)
306 
307     >>> TR2i(sin(x)**a/(cos(x) + 1)**a)
308     (cos(x) + 1)**(-a)*sin(x)**a
309 
310     """
311 
312     def f(rv):
313         if not rv.is_Mul:
314             return rv
315 
316         n, d = rv.as_numer_denom()
317         if n.is_Atom or d.is_Atom:
318             return rv
319 
320         def ok(k, e):
321             # initial filtering of factors
322             return (
323                 (e.is_integer or k.is_positive) and (
324                 k.func in (sin, cos) or (half and
325                 k.is_Add and
326                 len(k.args) >= 2 and
327                 any(any(isinstance(ai, cos) or ai.is_Pow and ai.base is cos
328                 for ai in Mul.make_args(a)) for a in k.args))))
329 
330         n = n.as_powers_dict()
331         ndone = [(k, n.pop(k)) for k in list(n.keys()) if not ok(k, n[k])]
332         if not n:
333             return rv
334 
335         d = d.as_powers_dict()
336         ddone = [(k, d.pop(k)) for k in list(d.keys()) if not ok(k, d[k])]
337         if not d:
338             return rv
339 
340         # factoring if necessary
341 
342         def factorize(d, ddone):
343             newk = []
344             for k in d:
345                 if k.is_Add and len(k.args) > 1:
346                     knew = factor(k) if half else factor_terms(k)
347                     if knew != k:
348                         newk.append((k, knew))
349             if newk:
350                 for i, (k, knew) in enumerate(newk):
351                     del d[k]
352                     newk[i] = knew
353                 newk = Mul(*newk).as_powers_dict()
354                 for k in newk:
355                     v = d[k] + newk[k]
356                     if ok(k, v):
357                         d[k] = v
358                     else:
359                         ddone.append((k, v))
360                 del newk
361         factorize(n, ndone)
362         factorize(d, ddone)
363 
364         # joining
365         t = []
366         for k in n:
367             if isinstance(k, sin):
368                 a = cos(k.args[0], evaluate=False)
369                 if a in d and d[a] == n[k]:
370                     t.append(tan(k.args[0])**n[k])
371                     n[k] = d[a] = None
372                 elif half:
373                     a1 = 1 + a
374                     if a1 in d and d[a1] == n[k]:
375                         t.append((tan(k.args[0]/2))**n[k])
376                         n[k] = d[a1] = None
377             elif isinstance(k, cos):
378                 a = sin(k.args[0], evaluate=False)
379                 if a in d and d[a] == n[k]:
380                     t.append(tan(k.args[0])**-n[k])
381                     n[k] = d[a] = None
382             elif half and k.is_Add and k.args[0] is S.One and \
383                     isinstance(k.args[1], cos):
384                 a = sin(k.args[1].args[0], evaluate=False)
385                 if a in d and d[a] == n[k] and (d[a].is_integer or \
386                         a.is_positive):
387                     t.append(tan(a.args[0]/2)**-n[k])
388                     n[k] = d[a] = None
389 
390         if t:
391             rv = Mul(*(t + [b**e for b, e in n.items() if e]))/\
392                 Mul(*[b**e for b, e in d.items() if e])
393             rv *= Mul(*[b**e for b, e in ndone])/Mul(*[b**e for b, e in ddone])
394 
395         return rv
396 
397     return bottom_up(rv, f)
398

400 def TR3(rv):
401     """Induced formula: example sin(-a) = -sin(a)
402 
403     Examples
404     ========
405 
406     >>> from sympy.simplify.fu import TR3
407     >>> from sympy.abc import x, y
408     >>> from sympy import pi
409     >>> from sympy import cos
410     >>> TR3(cos(y - x*(y - x)))
411     cos(x*(x - y) + y)
412     >>> cos(pi/2 + x)
413     -sin(x)
414     >>> cos(30*pi/2 + x)
415     -cos(x)
416 
417     """
418     from sympy.simplify.simplify import signsimp
419 
420     # Negative argument (already automatic for funcs like sin(-x) -> -sin(x)
421     # but more complicated expressions can use it, too). Also, trig angles
422     # between pi/4 and pi/2 are not reduced to an angle between 0 and pi/4.
423     # The following are automatically handled:
424     #   Argument of type: pi/2 +/- angle
425     #   Argument of type: pi +/- angle
426     #   Argument of type : 2k*pi +/- angle
427 
428     def f(rv):
429         if not isinstance(rv, TrigonometricFunction):
430             return rv
431         rv = rv.func(signsimp(rv.args[0]))
432         if not isinstance(rv, TrigonometricFunction):
433             return rv
434         if (rv.args[0] - S.Pi/4).is_positive is (S.Pi/2 - rv.args[0]).is_positive is True:
435             fmap = {cos: sin, sin: cos, tan: cot, cot: tan, sec: csc, csc: sec}
436             rv = fmap[rv.func](S.Pi/2 - rv.args[0])
437         return rv
438 
439     return bottom_up(rv, f)
440

470 def _TR56(rv, f, g, h, max, pow):
471     """Helper for TR5 and TR6 to replace f**2 with h(g**2)
472 
473     Options
474     =======
475 
476     max :   controls size of exponent that can appear on f
477             e.g. if max=4 then f**4 will be changed to h(g**2)**2.
478     pow :   controls whether the exponent must be a perfect power of 2
479             e.g. if pow=True (and max >= 6) then f**6 will not be changed
480             but f**8 will be changed to h(g**2)**4
481 
482     >>> from sympy.simplify.fu import _TR56 as T
483     >>> from sympy.abc import x
484     >>> from sympy import sin, cos
485     >>> h = lambda x: 1 - x
486     >>> T(sin(x)**3, sin, cos, h, 4, False)
487     sin(x)**3
488     >>> T(sin(x)**6, sin, cos, h, 6, False)
489     (1 - cos(x)**2)**3
490     >>> T(sin(x)**6, sin, cos, h, 6, True)
491     sin(x)**6
492     >>> T(sin(x)**8, sin, cos, h, 10, True)
493     (1 - cos(x)**2)**4
494     """
495 
496     def _f(rv):
497         # I'm not sure if this transformation should target all even powers
498         # or only those expressible as powers of 2. Also, should it only
499         # make the changes in powers that appear in sums -- making an isolated
500         # change is not going to allow a simplification as far as I can tell.
501         if not (rv.is_Pow and rv.base.func == f):
502             return rv
503 
504         if (rv.exp < 0) == True:
505             return rv
506         if (rv.exp > max) == True:
507             return rv
508         if rv.exp == 2:
509             return h(g(rv.base.args[0])**2)
510         else:
511             if rv.exp == 4:
512                 e = 2
513             elif not pow:
514                 if rv.exp % 2:
515                     return rv
516                 e = rv.exp//2
517             else:
518                 p = perfect_power(rv.exp)
519                 if not p:
520                     return rv
521                 e = rv.exp//2
522             return h(g(rv.base.args[0])**2)**e
523 
524     return bottom_up(rv, _f)
525

593 def TR8(rv, first=True):
594     """Converting products of ``cos`` and/or ``sin`` to a sum or
595     difference of ``cos`` and or ``sin`` terms.
596 
597     Examples
598     ========
599 
600     >>> from sympy.simplify.fu import TR8, TR7
601     >>> from sympy import cos, sin
602     >>> TR8(cos(2)*cos(3))
603     cos(5)/2 + cos(1)/2
604     >>> TR8(cos(2)*sin(3))
605     sin(5)/2 + sin(1)/2
606     >>> TR8(sin(2)*sin(3))
607     -cos(5)/2 + cos(1)/2
608     """
609 
610     def f(rv):
611         if not (
612             rv.is_Mul or
613             rv.is_Pow and
614             rv.base.func in (cos, sin) and
615             (rv.exp.is_integer or rv.base.is_positive)):
616             return rv
617 
618         if first:
619             n, d = [expand_mul(i) for i in rv.as_numer_denom()]
620             newn = TR8(n, first=False)
621             newd = TR8(d, first=False)
622             if newn != n or newd != d:
623                 rv = gcd_terms(newn/newd)
624                 if rv.is_Mul and rv.args[0].is_Rational and \
625                         len(rv.args) == 2 and rv.args[1].is_Add:
626                     rv = Mul(*rv.as_coeff_Mul())
627             return rv
628 
629         args = {cos: [], sin: [], None: []}
630         for a in ordered(Mul.make_args(rv)):
631             if a.func in (cos, sin):
632                 args[a.func].append(a.args[0])
633             elif (a.is_Pow and a.exp.is_Integer and a.exp > 0 and \
634                     a.base.func in (cos, sin)):
635                 # XXX this is ok but pathological expression could be handled
636                 # more efficiently as in TRmorrie
637                 args[a.base.func].extend([a.base.args[0]]*a.exp)
638             else:
639                 args[None].append(a)
640         c = args[cos]
641         s = args[sin]
642         if not (c and s or len(c) > 1 or len(s) > 1):
643             return rv
644 
645         args = args[None]
646         n = min(len(c), len(s))
647         for i in range(n):
648             a1 = s.pop()
649             a2 = c.pop()
650             args.append((sin(a1 + a2) + sin(a1 - a2))/2)
651         while len(c) > 1:
652             a1 = c.pop()
653             a2 = c.pop()
654             args.append((cos(a1 + a2) + cos(a1 - a2))/2)
655         if c:
656             args.append(cos(c.pop()))
657         while len(s) > 1:
658             a1 = s.pop()
659             a2 = s.pop()
660             args.append((-cos(a1 + a2) + cos(a1 - a2))/2)
661         if s:
662             args.append(sin(s.pop()))
663         return TR8(expand_mul(Mul(*args)))
664 
665     return bottom_up(rv, f)
666

668 def TR9(rv):
669     """Sum of ``cos`` or ``sin`` terms as a product of ``cos`` or ``sin``.
670 
671     Examples
672     ========
673 
674     >>> from sympy.simplify.fu import TR9
675     >>> from sympy import cos, sin
676     >>> TR9(cos(1) + cos(2))
677     2*cos(1/2)*cos(3/2)
678     >>> TR9(cos(1) + 2*sin(1) + 2*sin(2))
679     cos(1) + 4*sin(3/2)*cos(1/2)
680 
681     If no change is made by TR9, no re-arrangement of the
682     expression will be made. For example, though factoring
683     of common term is attempted, if the factored expression
684     wasn't changed, the original expression will be returned:
685 
686     >>> TR9(cos(3) + cos(3)*cos(2))
687     cos(3) + cos(2)*cos(3)
688 
689     """
690 
691     def f(rv):
692         if not rv.is_Add:
693             return rv
694 
695         def do(rv, first=True):
696             # cos(a)+/-cos(b) can be combined into a product of cosines and
697             # sin(a)+/-sin(b) can be combined into a product of cosine and
698             # sine.
699             #
700             # If there are more than two args, the pairs which "work" will
701             # have a gcd extractable and the remaining two terms will have
702             # the above structure -- all pairs must be checked to find the
703             # ones that work. args that don't have a common set of symbols
704             # are skipped since this doesn't lead to a simpler formula and
705             # also has the arbitrariness of combining, for example, the x
706             # and y term instead of the y and z term in something like
707             # cos(x) + cos(y) + cos(z).
708 
709             if not rv.is_Add:
710                 return rv
711 
712             args = list(ordered(rv.args))
713             if len(args) != 2:
714                 hit = False
715                 for i in range(len(args)):
716                     ai = args[i]
717                     if ai is None:
718                         continue
719                     for j in range(i + 1, len(args)):
720                         aj = args[j]
721                         if aj is None:
722                             continue
723                         was = ai + aj
724                         new = do(was)
725                         if new != was:
726                             args[i] = new  # update in place
727                             args[j] = None
728                             hit = True
729                             break  # go to next i
730                 if hit:
731                     rv = Add(*[_f for _f in args if _f])
732                     if rv.is_Add:
733                         rv = do(rv)
734 
735                 return rv
736 
737             # two-arg Add
738             split = trig_split(*args)
739             if not split:
740                 return rv
741             gcd, n1, n2, a, b, iscos = split
742 
743             # application of rule if possible
744             if iscos:
745                 if n1 == n2:
746                     return gcd*n1*2*cos((a + b)/2)*cos((a - b)/2)
747                 if n1 < 0:
748                     a, b = b, a
749                 return -2*gcd*sin((a + b)/2)*sin((a - b)/2)
750             else:
751                 if n1 == n2:
752                     return gcd*n1*2*sin((a + b)/2)*cos((a - b)/2)
753                 if n1 < 0:
754                     a, b = b, a
755                 return 2*gcd*cos((a + b)/2)*sin((a - b)/2)
756 
757         return process_common_addends(rv, do)  # DON'T sift by free symbols
758 
759     return bottom_up(rv, f)
760

762 def TR10(rv, first=True):
763     """Separate sums in ``cos`` and ``sin``.
764 
765     Examples
766     ========
767 
768     >>> from sympy.simplify.fu import TR10
769     >>> from sympy.abc import a, b, c
770     >>> from sympy import cos, sin
771     >>> TR10(cos(a + b))
772     -sin(a)*sin(b) + cos(a)*cos(b)
773     >>> TR10(sin(a + b))
774     sin(a)*cos(b) + sin(b)*cos(a)
775     >>> TR10(sin(a + b + c))
776     (-sin(a)*sin(b) + cos(a)*cos(b))*sin(c) + \
777     (sin(a)*cos(b) + sin(b)*cos(a))*cos(c)
778     """
779 
780     def f(rv):
781         if not rv.func in (cos, sin):
782             return rv
783 
784         f = rv.func
785         arg = rv.args[0]
786         if arg.is_Add:
787             if first:
788                 args = list(ordered(arg.args))
789             else:
790                 args = list(arg.args)
791             a = args.pop()
792             b = Add._from_args(args)
793             if b.is_Add:
794                 if f == sin:
795                     return sin(a)*TR10(cos(b), first=False) + \
796                         cos(a)*TR10(sin(b), first=False)
797                 else:
798                     return cos(a)*TR10(cos(b), first=False) - \
799                         sin(a)*TR10(sin(b), first=False)
800             else:
801                 if f == sin:
802                     return sin(a)*cos(b) + cos(a)*sin(b)
803                 else:
804                     return cos(a)*cos(b) - sin(a)*sin(b)
805         return rv
806 
807     return bottom_up(rv, f)

810 def TR10i(rv):
811     """Sum of products to function of sum.
812 
813     Examples
814     ========
815 
816     >>> from sympy.simplify.fu import TR10i
817     >>> from sympy import cos, sin, pi, Add, Mul, sqrt, Symbol
818     >>> from sympy.abc import x, y
819 
820     >>> TR10i(cos(1)*cos(3) + sin(1)*sin(3))
821     cos(2)
822     >>> TR10i(cos(1)*sin(3) + sin(1)*cos(3) + cos(3))
823     cos(3) + sin(4)
824     >>> TR10i(sqrt(2)*cos(x)*x + sqrt(6)*sin(x)*x)
825     2*sqrt(2)*x*sin(x + pi/6)
826 
827     """
828     global _ROOT2, _ROOT3, _invROOT3
829     if _ROOT2 is None:
830         _roots()
831 
832     def f(rv):
833         if not rv.is_Add:
834             return rv
835 
836         def do(rv, first=True):
837             # args which can be expressed as A*(cos(a)*cos(b)+/-sin(a)*sin(b))
838             # or B*(cos(a)*sin(b)+/-cos(b)*sin(a)) can be combined into
839             # A*f(a+/-b) where f is either sin or cos.
840             #
841             # If there are more than two args, the pairs which "work" will have
842             # a gcd extractable and the remaining two terms will have the above
843             # structure -- all pairs must be checked to find the ones that
844             # work.
845 
846             if not rv.is_Add:
847                 return rv
848 
849             args = list(ordered(rv.args))
850             if len(args) != 2:
851                 hit = False
852                 for i in range(len(args)):
853                     ai = args[i]
854                     if ai is None:
855                         continue
856                     for j in range(i + 1, len(args)):
857                         aj = args[j]
858                         if aj is None:
859                             continue
860                         was = ai + aj
861                         new = do(was)
862                         if new != was:
863                             args[i] = new  # update in place
864                             args[j] = None
865                             hit = True
866                             break  # go to next i
867                 if hit:
868                     rv = Add(*[_f for _f in args if _f])
869                     if rv.is_Add:
870                         rv = do(rv)
871 
872                 return rv
873 
874             # two-arg Add
875             split = trig_split(*args, two=True)
876             if not split:
877                 return rv
878             gcd, n1, n2, a, b, same = split
879 
880             # identify and get c1 to be cos then apply rule if possible
881             if same:  # coscos, sinsin
882                 gcd = n1*gcd
883                 if n1 == n2:
884                     return gcd*cos(a - b)
885                 return gcd*cos(a + b)
886             else:  #cossin, cossin
887                 gcd = n1*gcd
888                 if n1 == n2:
889                     return gcd*sin(a + b)
890                 return gcd*sin(b - a)
891 
892         rv = process_common_addends(
893             rv, do, lambda x: tuple(ordered(x.free_symbols)))
894 
895         # need to check for inducible pairs in ratio of sqrt(3):1 that
896         # appeared in different lists when sorting by coefficient
897         while rv.is_Add:
898             byrad = defaultdict(list)
899             for a in rv.args:
900                 hit = 0
901                 if a.is_Mul:
902                     for ai in a.args:
903                         if ai.is_Pow and ai.exp is S.Half and \
904                                 ai.base.is_Integer:
905                             byrad[ai].append(a)
906                             hit = 1
907                             break
908                 if not hit:
909                     byrad[S.One].append(a)
910 
911             # no need to check all pairs -- just check for the onees
912             # that have the right ratio
913             args = []
914             for a in byrad:
915                 for b in [_ROOT3*a, _invROOT3]:
916                     if b in byrad:
917                         for i in range(len(byrad[a])):
918                             if byrad[a][i] is None:
919                                 continue
920                             for j in range(len(byrad[b])):
921                                 if byrad[b][j] is None:
922                                     continue
923                                 was = Add(byrad[a][i] + byrad[b][j])
924                                 new = do(was)
925                                 if new != was:
926                                     args.append(new)
927                                     byrad[a][i] = None
928                                     byrad[b][j] = None
929                                     break
930             if args:
931                 rv = Add(*(args + [Add(*[_f for _f in v if _f])
932                     for v in byrad.values()]))
933             else:
934                 rv = do(rv)  # final pass to resolve any new inducible pairs
935                 break
936 
937         return rv
938 
939     return bottom_up(rv, f)

958     4*(-sin(x)**2 + cos(x)**2)*sin(x)*cos(x)
959     >>> TR11(sin(4*x/3))
960     4*(-sin(x/3)**2 + cos(x/3)**2)*sin(x/3)*cos(x/3)

963     unless a base is provided:

967     >>> TR11(cos(4), 2)

969 
970     There is a subtle issue here in that autosimplification will convert
971     some higher angles to lower angles

973     >>> cos(6*pi/7) + cos(3*pi/7)

977     the 3*pi/7 base:

985         if not rv.func in (cos, sin):
986             return rv

988         if base:
989             f = rv.func
990             t = f(base*2)
991             co = S.One
992             if t.is_Mul:
993                 co, t = t.as_coeff_Mul()
994             if not t.func in (cos, sin):
995                 return rv
996             if rv.args[0] == t.args[0]:
997                 c = cos(base)
998                 s = sin(base)
999                 if f is cos:
1000                     return (c**2 - s**2)/co
1001                 else:
1002                     return 2*c*s/co
1003             return rv
1004 
1005         elif not rv.args[0].is_Number:
1006             # make a change if the leading coefficient's numerator is
1007             # divisible by 2

1014                     rv = 2*s*c
1015                 else:
1016                     rv = c**2 - s**2

1230 def TRmorrie(rv):

1233     Examples
1234     ========

1236     >>> from sympy.simplify.fu import TRmorrie, TR8, TR3
1237     >>> from sympy.abc import x
1238     >>> from sympy import Mul, cos, pi
1239     >>> TRmorrie(cos(x)*cos(2*x))
1240     sin(4*x)/(4*sin(x))
1241     >>> TRmorrie(7*Mul(*[cos(x) for x in range(10)]))
1242     7*sin(12)*sin(16)*cos(5)*cos(7)*cos(9)/(64*sin(1)*sin(3))

1244     Sometimes autosimplification will cause a power to be
1245     not recognized. e.g. in the following, cos(4*pi/7) automatically
1246     simplifies to -cos(3*pi/7) so only 2 of the 3 terms are
1247     recognized:
1248 
1249     >>> TRmorrie(cos(pi/7)*cos(2*pi/7)*cos(4*pi/7))
1250     -sin(3*pi/7)*cos(3*pi/7)/(4*sin(pi/7))

1253 
1254     >>> TR8(_)
1255     -1/8

1258     directly:
1259 
1260     >>> eq = cos(pi/9)*cos(2*pi/9)*cos(3*pi/9)*cos(4*pi/9)
1261     >>> TRmorrie(eq)
1262     1/16
1263 
1264     But if angles are made canonical with TR3 then the answer
1265     is not simplified without further work:
1266 
1267     >>> TR3(eq)
1268     sin(pi/18)*cos(pi/9)*cos(2*pi/9)/2
1269     >>> TRmorrie(_)
1270     sin(pi/18)*sin(4*pi/9)/(8*sin(pi/9))
1271     >>> TR8(_)
1272     cos(7*pi/18)/(16*sin(pi/9))
1273     >>> TR3(_)
1274     1/16
1275 
1276     The original expression would have resolve to 1/16 directly with TR8,
1277     however:
1278 
1279     >>> TR8(eq)
1280     1/16
1281 
1282     References
1283     ==========
1284 
1285     https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrie%27s_law
1286 
1287     """

1289     def f(rv, first=True):
1290         if not rv.is_Mul:
1291             return rv
1292         if first:
1293             n, d = rv.as_numer_denom()
1294             return f(n, 0)/f(d, 0)
1295 
1296         args = defaultdict(list)
1297         coss = {}
1298         other = []
1299         for c in rv.args:
1300             b, e = c.as_base_exp()
1301             if e.is_Integer and isinstance(b, cos):
1302                 co, a = b.args[0].as_coeff_Mul()
1303                 args[a].append(co)
1304                 coss[b] = e
1305             else:
1306                 other.append(c)
1307 
1308         new = []
1309         for a in args:
1310             c = args[a]
1311             c.sort()
1312             no = []
1313             while c:
1314                 k = 0
1315                 cc = ci = c[0]
1316                 while cc in c:
1317                     k += 1
1318                     cc *= 2
1319                 if k > 1:
1320                     newarg = sin(2**k*ci*a)/2**k/sin(ci*a)
1321                     # see how many times this can be taken
1322                     take = None
1323                     ccs = []
1324                     for i in range(k):
1325                         cc /= 2
1326                         key = cos(a*cc, evaluate=False)
1327                         ccs.append(cc)
1328                         take = min(coss[key], take or coss[key])
1329                     # update exponent counts
1330                     for i in range(k):
1331                         cc = ccs.pop()
1332                         key = cos(a*cc, evaluate=False)
1333                         coss[key] -= take
1334                         if not coss[key]:
1335                             c.remove(cc)
1336                     new.append(newarg**take)
1337                 else:
1338                     no.append(c.pop(0))
1339             c[:] = no
1340 
1341         if new:
1342             rv = Mul(*(new + other + [
1343                 cos(k*a, evaluate=False) for a in args for k in args[a]]))
1344 
1345         return rv
1346

1350 def TR14(rv, first=True):

1355     ========

1358     >>> from sympy.abc import x, y

1361     -sin(x)**2
1362     >>> TR14((sin(x) - 1)*(sin(x) + 1))
1363     -cos(x)**2
1364     >>> p1 = (cos(x) + 1)*(cos(x) - 1)
1365     >>> p2 = (cos(y) - 1)*2*(cos(y) + 1)
1366     >>> p3 = (3*(cos(y) - 1))*(3*(cos(y) + 1))
1367     >>> TR14(p1*p2*p3*(x - 1))
1368     -18*(x - 1)*sin(x)**2*sin(y)**4
1369

1372     def f(rv):
1373         if not rv.is_Mul:
1374             return rv
1375 
1376         if first:
1377             # sort them by location in numerator and denominator
1378             # so the code below can just deal with positive exponents
1379             n, d = rv.as_numer_denom()
1380             if d is not S.One:
1381                 newn = TR14(n, first=False)
1382                 newd = TR14(d, first=False)
1383                 if newn != n or newd != d:
1384                     rv = newn/newd
1385                 return rv
1386 
1387         other = []
1388         process = []
1389         for a in rv.args:
1390             if a.is_Pow:
1391                 b, e = a.as_base_exp()
1392                 if not (e.is_integer or b.is_positive):
1393                     other.append(a)
1394                     continue
1395                 a = b
1396             else:
1397                 e = S.One
1398             m = as_f_sign_1(a)
1399             if not m or m[1].func not in (cos, sin):
1400                 if e is S.One:
1401                     other.append(a)
1402                 else:
1403                     other.append(a**e)
1404                 continue
1405             g, f, si = m
1406             process.append((g, e.is_Number, e, f, si, a))
1407 
1408         # sort them to get like terms next to each other
1409         process = list(ordered(process))
1410 
1411         # keep track of whether there was any change
1412         nother = len(other)
1413 
1414         # access keys
1415         keys = (g, t, e, f, si, a) = list(range(6))
1416 
1417         while process:
1418             A = process.pop(0)
1419             if process:
1420                 B = process[0]
1421 
1422                 if A[e].is_Number and B[e].is_Number:
1423                     # both exponents are numbers
1424                     if A[f] == B[f]:
1425                         if A[si] != B[si]:
1426                             B = process.pop(0)
1427                             take = min(A[e], B[e])
1428 
1429                             # reinsert any remainder
1430                             # the B will likely sort after A so check it first
1431                             if B[e] != take:
1432                                 rem = [B[i] for i in keys]
1433                                 rem[e] -= take
1434                                 process.insert(0, rem)
1435                             elif A[e] != take:
1436                                 rem = [A[i] for i in keys]
1437                                 rem[e] -= take
1438                                 process.insert(0, rem)
1439 
1440                             if isinstance(A[f], cos):
1441                                 t = sin
1442                             else:
1443                                 t = cos
1444                             other.append((-A[g]*B[g]*t(A[f].args[0])**2)**take)
1445                             continue
1446 
1447                 elif A[e] == B[e]:
1448                     # both exponents are equal symbols
1449                     if A[f] == B[f]:
1450                         if A[si] != B[si]:
1451                             B = process.pop(0)
1452                             take = A[e]
1453                             if isinstance(A[f], cos):
1454                                 t = sin
1455                             else:
1456                                 t = cos
1457                             other.append((-A[g]*B[g]*t(A[f].args[0])**2)**take)
1458                             continue
1459 
1460             # either we are done or neither condition above applied
1461             other.append(A[a]**A[e])
1462 
1463         if len(other) != nother:
1464             rv = Mul(*other)
1465 
1466         return rv
1467 
1468     return bottom_up(rv, f)

250                 sexpr, rat_expo = exp(tail), coeff
251         elif isinstance(expr, Derivative):
252             sexpr, deriv = parse_derivative(expr)
253 
254         return sexpr, rat_expo, sym_expo, deriv
255 
256     def parse_expression(terms, pattern):
257         """Parse terms searching for a pattern.
258         terms is a list of tuples as returned by parse_terms;
259         pattern is an expression treated as a product of factors
260         """
261         pattern = Mul.make_args(pattern)
262 
263         if len(terms) < len(pattern):
264             # pattern is longer than matched product
265             # so no chance for positive parsing result
266             return None
267         else:
268             pattern = [parse_term(elem) for elem in pattern]
269 
270             terms = terms[:]  # need a copy
271             elems, common_expo, has_deriv = [], None, False
272 
273             for elem, e_rat, e_sym, e_ord in pattern:
274 
275                 if elem.is_Number and e_rat == 1 and e_sym is None:
276                     # a constant is a match for everything
277                     continue
278 
279                 for j in range(len(terms)):
280                     if terms[j] is None:
281                         continue
282 
283                     term, t_rat, t_sym, t_ord = terms[j]
284 
285                     # keeping track of whether one of the terms had
286                     # a derivative or not as this will require rebuilding
287                     # the expression later
288                     if t_ord is not None:
289                         has_deriv = True
290 
291                     if (term.match(elem) is not None and
292                             (t_sym == e_sym or t_sym is not None and
293                             e_sym is not None and
294                             t_sym.match(e_sym) is not None)):
295                         if exact is False:
296                             # we don't have to be exact so find common exponent
297                             # for both expression's term and pattern's element
298                             expo = t_rat / e_rat
299 
300                             if common_expo is None:
301                                 # first time
302                                 common_expo = expo
303                             else:
304                                 # common exponent was negotiated before so
305                                 # there is no chance for a pattern match unless
306                                 # common and current exponents are equal
307                                 if common_expo != expo:
308                                     common_expo = 1
309                         else:
310                             # we ought to be exact so all fields of
311                             # interest must match in every details
312                             if e_rat != t_rat or e_ord != t_ord:
313                                 continue
314 
315                         # found common term so remove it from the expression
316                         # and try to match next element in the pattern
317                         elems.append(terms[j])
318                         terms[j] = None
319 
320                         break
321 
322                 else:
323                     # pattern element not found
324                     return None
325 
326             return [_f for _f in terms if _f], elems, common_expo, has_deriv
327 
328     if evaluate:
329         if expr.is_Add:
330             o = expr.getO() or 0
331             expr = expr.func(*[
332                     collect(a, syms, func, True, exact, distribute_order_term)
333                     for a in expr.args if a != o]) + o
334         elif expr.is_Mul:
335             return expr.func(*[
336                 collect(term, syms, func, True, exact, distribute_order_term)
337                 for term in expr.args])
338         elif expr.is_Pow:
339             b = collect(
340                 expr.base, syms, func, True, exact, distribute_order_term)
341             return Pow(b, expr.exp)
342 
343     syms = [expand_power_base(i, deep=False) for i in syms]
344 
345     order_term = None
346 
347     if distribute_order_term:
348         order_term = expr.getO()
349 
350         if order_term is not None:
351             if order_term.has(*syms):
352                 order_term = None
353             else:
354                 expr = expr.removeO()
355 
356     summa = [expand_power_base(i, deep=False) for i in Add.make_args(expr)]
357 
358     collected, disliked = defaultdict(list), S.Zero
359     for product in summa:
360         c, nc = product.args_cnc(split_1=False)
361         args = list(ordered(c)) + nc
362         terms = [parse_term(i) for i in args]
363         small_first = True
364 
365         for symbol in syms:
366             if SYMPY_DEBUG:
367                 print("DEBUG: parsing of expression %s with symbol %s " % (
368                     str(terms), str(symbol))
369                 )
370 
371             if isinstance(symbol, Derivative) and small_first:
372                 terms = list(reversed(terms))
373                 small_first = not small_first
374             result = parse_expression(terms, symbol)
375 
376             if SYMPY_DEBUG:
377                 print("DEBUG: returned %s" % str(result))
378 
379             if result is not None:
380                 if not symbol.is_commutative:
381                     raise AttributeError("Can not collect noncommutative symbol")
382 
383                 terms, elems, common_expo, has_deriv = result
384 
385                 # when there was derivative in current pattern we
386                 # will need to rebuild its expression from scratch
387                 if not has_deriv:
388                     margs = []
389                     for elem in elems:
390                         if elem[2] is None:
391                             e = elem[1]
392                         else:
393                             e = elem[1]*elem[2]
394                         margs.append(Pow(elem[0], e))
395                     index = Mul(*margs)
396                 else:
397                     index = make_expression(elems)
398                 terms = expand_power_base(make_expression(terms), deep=False)
399                 index = expand_power_base(index, deep=False)
400                 collected[index].append(terms)
401                 break
402         else:
403             # none of the patterns matched
404             disliked += product
405     # add terms now for each key
406     collected = {k: Add(*v) for k, v in collected.items()}
407 
408     if disliked is not S.Zero:
409         collected[S.One] = disliked
410 
411     if order_term is not None:
412         for key, val in collected.items():
413             collected[key] = val + order_term
414 
415     if func is not None:
416         collected = dict(
417             [(key, func(val)) for key, val in collected.items()])
418 
419     if evaluate:
420         return Add(*[key*val for key, val in collected.items()])
421     else:
422         return collected
423

425 def rcollect(expr, *vars):
426     """
427     Recursively collect sums in an expression.
428 
429     Examples
430     ========
431 
432     >>> from sympy.simplify import rcollect
433     >>> from sympy.abc import x, y
434 
435     >>> expr = (x**2*y + x*y + x + y)/(x + y)
436 
437     >>> rcollect(expr, y)
438     (x + y*(x**2 + x + 1))/(x + y)
439 
440     See Also
441     ========
442 
443     collect, collect_const, collect_sqrt
444     """
445     if expr.is_Atom or not expr.has(*vars):
446         return expr
447     else:
448         expr = expr.__class__(*[rcollect(arg, *vars) for arg in expr.args])
449 
450         if expr.is_Add:
451             return collect(expr, vars)
452         else:
453             return expr

456 def collect_sqrt(expr, evaluate=None):
457     """Return expr with terms having common square roots collected together.
458     If ``evaluate`` is False a count indicating the number of sqrt-containing
459     terms will be returned and, if non-zero, the terms of the Add will be
460     returned, else the expression itself will be returned as a single term.
461     If ``evaluate`` is True, the expression with any collected terms will be
462     returned.
463 
464     Note: since I = sqrt(-1), it is collected, too.
465 
466     Examples
467     ========
468 
469     >>> from sympy import sqrt
470     >>> from sympy.simplify.radsimp import collect_sqrt
471     >>> from sympy.abc import a, b
472 
473     >>> r2, r3, r5 = [sqrt(i) for i in [2, 3, 5]]
474     >>> collect_sqrt(a*r2 + b*r2)
475     sqrt(2)*(a + b)
476     >>> collect_sqrt(a*r2 + b*r2 + a*r3 + b*r3)
477     sqrt(2)*(a + b) + sqrt(3)*(a + b)
478     >>> collect_sqrt(a*r2 + b*r2 + a*r3 + b*r5)
479     sqrt(3)*a + sqrt(5)*b + sqrt(2)*(a + b)
480 
481     If evaluate is False then the arguments will be sorted and
482     returned as a list and a count of the number of sqrt-containing
483     terms will be returned:
484 
485     >>> collect_sqrt(a*r2 + b*r2 + a*r3 + b*r5, evaluate=False)
486     ((sqrt(3)*a, sqrt(5)*b, sqrt(2)*(a + b)), 3)
487     >>> collect_sqrt(a*sqrt(2) + b, evaluate=False)
488     ((b, sqrt(2)*a), 1)
489     >>> collect_sqrt(a + b, evaluate=False)
490     ((a + b,), 0)
491 
492     See Also
493     ========
494 
495     collect, collect_const, rcollect
496     """
497     if evaluate is None:
498         evaluate = global_evaluate[0]
499     # this step will help to standardize any complex arguments
500     # of sqrts
501     coeff, expr = expr.as_content_primitive()
502     vars = set()
503     for a in Add.make_args(expr):
504         for m in a.args_cnc()[0]:
505             if m.is_number and (
506                     m.is_Pow and m.exp.is_Rational and m.exp.q == 2 or
507                     m is S.ImaginaryUnit):
508                 vars.add(m)
509 
510     # we only want radicals, so exclude Number handling; in this case
511     # d will be evaluated
512     d = collect_const(expr, *vars, Numbers=False)
513     hit = expr != d
514 
515     if not evaluate:
516         nrad = 0
517         # make the evaluated args canonical
518         args = list(ordered(Add.make_args(d)))
519         for i, m in enumerate(args):
520             c, nc = m.args_cnc()
521             for ci in c:
522                 # XXX should this be restricted to ci.is_number as above?
523                 if ci.is_Pow and ci.exp.is_Rational and ci.exp.q == 2 or \
524                         ci is S.ImaginaryUnit:
525                     nrad += 1
526                     break
527             args[i] *= coeff
528         if not (hit or nrad):
529             args = [Add(*args)]
530         return tuple(args), nrad
531 
532     return coeff*d
533
